GRAHAM: In order that the Bill in connection with the Canadian Northern may be expedited, I would ask the Minister of Finance-in his absence, the Prime Minister-to bring down a statement showing how much had been paid by the Canadian Northern Railway company on interest account under section 29 of the Act of 1914 and how much money the Government had advanced on that interest account. Section 29 reads:
The Governor in Council may at the request of the Canadian Northern out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund pay all or any portion of the first six half-yearly payments of interest on the guaranteed securities falling due after the opening for traffic as part of the Canadian Northern system of the through line from Vancouver to the city of Quebec, but in suchl case the Governor in Council shall not enforce the repayment thereof against the Canadian Northern under the New Trust Deed until the maturity of the principal of the guaranteed securities. The Canadian Northern shall, however, pending the repayment of interest so, paid by the Governor in Council, pay to His Majesty half-yearly interest on such interest at the rate of four per cent per annum, and such interest upon interest until so paid shall form a charge upon the mortgaged premises under the New Trust Deed.
What I want to know is how much money the Government paid out on this account and how much money the company paid as interest on the interest so advanced by the Government.

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.

speechtext:
On motion of Hon. Frank Cochrane (Minister of Railways and Canals) Bill No. 118, to amend the Government Railways Act, was read the second time and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Davidson in the Chair.
On section 2-Definition:

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Will the minister explain the purport and effect of this measure?

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: The effect of the Bill is to put the Government railways under the operation of the Railway Commission. Everything is put under the control of the commission except the expropriation clauses; and .any actions taken against the railway go to the Exchequer Court instead of being dealt with in the usual manner.

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Has the minister received any representations from persons or interests in the Maritime Provinces asking that this be done?

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: No, I have not.

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Or any against it?

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: No.

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
This measure is a very important one, affecting the business interests of the Maritime Provinces and I
think that more notice should have been given to the public of the Government's intention to deal with it. In view of the other subjects that have been engaging the attention of Parliament, the people of the Maritime Provinces are not familiar with this very important measure which the minister is introducing.
In brief, it is an anomalous position that the Government which owns and has been operating a public utility and which still purposes operating it, should create a condition under which an outside body should form a sort of regulating influence upon the Government of the day. One can well understand the reason why a private company controlling a railway should be placed under the supervision and regulation of a commission. The Board of Railway Commissioners, which has been in operation for some ten years, was constituted so that the public might have the advantage of the control and regulation which a commission would have over the operations of a private company which was handling a great enterprise. The minister now says that the Government which owns and operates the Canadian Government railways, are not able to deal with this question themselves, but they must create a commission which is to direct and control them in reference to certain matters concerning the operation of this railway. That is an anomalous position and one which is entirely new in the realm of government ownership and operation of public utilities, concerning which we hear so much nowadays. Does the minister mean to say that he has no confidence in himself or in his officials, and that he must, therefore, have the benefit and advantage of the control of Sir Henry Drayton and his officials in order to properly operate this railway, because that is what is involved in this Bill?
There is another phase of the situation. The Intercolonial railway is the only railway in Canady which was constituted by virtue of the terms of the British North America Act. It will be recalled that, what were at the time of Confederation these far away provinces of the Dominion, viewed, with some doubt and misgiving, the proposition of entering the Confederation by reason of the effect that would have upon their business interests, and the scheme of constructing what was known as the Intercolonial railway was put forward by the Fathers of Confederation for the purpose of doing .away with the isolation by distance of the Maritime Provinces from the



then central provinces of Canada. The viewpoint of the people of the Maritime Provinces-particularly of the province from which I come, where our industries arising out of our natural resources are of such character that to a very great degree our products so far as the markets of Canada are concerned, must be transported over the Intercolonial railway-has been that the extension of that railway as a government work, on account of the conditions which exist in consequence of the Government of the day being responsible to the people and thereby able to deal with particular matters as they may, from time to time, arise, and it is a matter which is not lightly to be disregarded. I have never heard of any agitation from any part of the Maritime Provinces that this railway should be dealt with in such a way that the Government should be under the control of the Board of Railway Commissioners, and the proposition will be viewed with a considerable degree of doubt and hesitancy by the people of those provinces. I am, therefore, surprised that at this juncture, without any preparation of the public mind on the subject, without apparently the interests affected in those provinces being considered, the minister should take such a radical step. It is due to the House and to the country that the minister or his colleagues should explain in the fullest possible manner the reasons that have led the Government to take this course, and why it is that the Government of this country want to subordinate themselves, in so far as the operation of a public utility is concerned, to the Railway Commission. Is there any reason why my hon. friend, as Minister of Railways, or his officials, could not, with regard to any phase of the operation of the Canadian Government railways, if there is any advantage to be gained by so doing, exercise this same supervision which is conferred upon the Railway Commission? This is the first time that I have ever heard of a Government of a country, which was operating a public utility, declare that they required some watch-dog to look after them, or somebody who should dictate to them what they should do. If this is to be the case with the operation of the Canadian Government railways, why should there not, for instance, be in regard to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries some board to direct and control what his movements should be as regards the operation of the vessels belonging to his department? Why should there be anybody 
greater or stronger than the Government of the day who should undertake to tell the Government that they should do this, that, or the other thing? Why should the Government not move in the interest of the people themselves?
In view of the absence of any suggestion from the provinces affected, and in view of the fact that the minister has never submitted the matter to the people in those provinces, I am at a loss to know why the Government should make this proposition at this time, to a very large degree in a surreptitious way. Neither the press nor the people of this country ever heard of this proposition until it w.as mentioned in this House the other day.

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: As regards our not giving any notice of this proposition or of its not having been discussed, I may say that the hon. member was * member of the special committee on Bill No. 13. This matter was discussed several times in that committee, and it was urged by some hon. gentleman opposite. The matter has been discussed more or less ever since I have been in this House, and I therefore cannot take the same view as that taken by my hon. friend from Pietou (Mr. Macdonald). No matter what minister may be operating that line, there will always be a difference of opinion between him and the patrons of the road, and I think we should have this safeguard, especially as it looks as though the Government were going into further government ownership. Therefore, the more independently those government lines can be operated, the better it will be in the interest of the country. I certainly am a strong advocate of this proposition. The Railway Board is a splendid institution in the interest of this country, and as long as I am Minister of Railways, I am willing to go under their direction and to abide by and obey their decisions. The only reason why I am not putting the expropriation of lands under their control is because the Exchequer Court was created for that purpose. I am sure a number of my hon. friend's colleagues on his side of the House will agree with me that this proposition is in the public interest.

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I am very sorry to be compelled to disagree with my hon. friend from Pietou (Mr. Macdonald), whose views on public matters are usually orthodox, but I must differ from him on the question of placing the government railways under the control of the Railway Board. My only objection is that the minister is not going

far enough. Possibly there may be some reason for withholding from the operation of the Railway Act the expropriation rights. I can quite understand that if the Crown wishes to acquire property or land, possibly the better way for the Government to obtain it is under the Expropriation Act. Then the damages are assessed by the Exchequer Court. I think possibly, so far as the Crown is concerned, it works out better than the ordinary arbitration proceedings under the Railway Act, but I never could understand why, if the Government is going to be a railway company, and is going to assume all the rights and duties of a railway company, they should not also be liable for all the obligations' of a company, because, so far as the people 'are concerned, they are simply a public utility corporation. They have the right to build their road, levy tolls, run their engines through the country, and burn up people's property as an incident of operating a railway. You cannot run a railway by fire without having the danger by fire, or without the danger of killing the people's stock.

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: We are providing for that.

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I realize that in small actions we already have the right to sue the Government in the ordinary courts of the country, but I cannot see why there should be. any distinction between suing the Government in the small action and suing them in a large action. I think the amount is now limited to $400.

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I had a case within the last few months which illustrates this point very well1. A man living up at St. Leonard, in New Brunswick, had a barn burned in the spring of 1916, and there is not the faintest doubt in the world that the barn was set on fire by a spark from an engine on the Intercolonial, because the engine went by, and in about ten minutes the barn was on fire and consumed. The value of the property lost amounted to about $1,000.

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: That proposition would not carry you through a logical school, would it?

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: We have won lots of cases under just such circumstances.

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: That is the way the lawyer gets along. *

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
No wonder they kick on the judges.
275J

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
The circumstances I
have related are good evidence. I have won cases on just such evidence, .and other counsel have succeeded on similar evidence. It is .a good cause of action. But the difficulty was, here was a poor farmer, ,and I had to advise him that, unless he reduced his claim to $500, his only recourse was to sue the Government in the Exchequer Court. He wo.uld have to see the Minister of Justice and get a fiat authorizing him to bring the suit. Then he had to fight it out in Ottawa. The man said to me: "I will lose my farm. It is out of the .question. I could not do it." I do not want to go so far as to say that I advised him to start the lawsuit, but at any rate he would not do it, because he said " I am not .going to take chances of losing all the rest of my farm. I have lost my barn and .my personal property, but I want to keep my farm." I wrote to the minister and it was referred to the general manager, and be sent somebody up there a second time. They sent the claims agent who turned the thing down in the first instance, and I do not know whether they have settled or not. I think they have arranged the matter. However, that is a case in point. If we can bring an action in the ordinary courts up to $500, why on earth should we not use them for $1,000 or $5,000? Surely the ordinary courts of any province in Canada are to be	trusted in	an action against
the Crown, just as well as the Exchequer Court is trusted. The litigants and solicitors all over Canada know the practice and know their rights. You can tell a man in the province of New Brunswick :	" I can bring an action for you in
the Supreme Court of New Brunswick; it will be tried at home, under our ordinary laws and! rules." And he will say: ."All right, I am sure I will get justice." And hie brings the action.	But if you
tell him he has to go to Ottawa and get the consent of the Minister of Justice before he can start his suit, and that it must be tried by the Exchequer Court, he says, " No, that is beyond my means," and he will not do it. For these reasons I think the Minister of Justice might very well consider the advisability of not withdrawing from the operation of this Bill suits against the Crown. If he wishes to withdraw the right of expropriation, I have not much objection. As to the general principle, .perhaps I ought to state that I think I was the first member to suggest, in the proceedings of the special

committee on Bill 13, for the codification of the Railway Aot, that the Intercolonial should be brought under the operation of the General Railway Act of Canada. I have heard very much discussion about it, I do not know whether it would be popular or unpopular in the Maritime Provinces, because it has not been discussed to any great extent, and I was not approaching it from that standpoint at all, but from the standpoint of one who has had some practice in the courts, and some knowledge of railway affairs, and I do not see why one railway should be singled out in Canada to be governed by different laws and different principles from those that govern all other railways in Canada, especially as it is a government railway. There is no earthly difference in the object of the Intercolonial and that of any other railway. The object ought to be to serve the public at a fair remuneration, and give the people the very best service which possibly can be given for the money. I am not finding fault with the present minister in what I am going to say, because his conduct, or his operation of the road, is only a continu-, ation of what has taken place for a great many years. Therefore, there is no political significance in this statement.
I think I am voicing the sentiments of every hon. gentleman in this House who has travelled and has had business with the Intercolonial, and with other railway companies, when I say that everybody admits that a very unsatisfactory condition of things exists, as far as the Intercolonial is concerned. Yon are tied up by all sorts of rules and regulations. If you want a siding put in on the Intercolonial it will take you six months before you can obtain consent to it, because the first man you go to will put the responsibility on somebody else, and then the second man will put the responsibility on .somebody else, *and finally, after a process of elimination, they will get it back to the minister, and the minister eliminates everybody else' and gets it back to the general manager, and probably at the end of six months you might get a decision, and I would not say that you would get what you want. There ought to be some way by which you could go to a board like the Railway Board and let them lay down the law. They would say that the Government of Canada, if they are going to be a railway company,ought or ought not to give the man the accommodation which he demands. Get away from all political feeling, and give the people to understand that politicians have nothing to 
say about it. Under the ordinary railway law, if you want a siding, or a right to establish a certain thing, or if a certain right be taken away from you, you go to the Railway Board, and they will say yes, or no, and they will say it in about five minutes. The first time I appeared before the Railway Board I complained of the Canadian Pacific railway taiking a siding away from the warehouse of a client of mine, and I came there armed with quite a brief, and witnesses .to substantiate the case, and 1 got the decision before I knew it.

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Did you get a fee?

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Yes, and the siding.

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Very much disappointed?

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I got what I was after before I knew it. That is the w.ay business is done by the Railway Board. If that had been a government railway I would not have got the decision yet, and that is eight or ten years ago. I give this illustration to show the great benefit of having these matters under the Railway Board, instead of under a political management. I do not care whether it be my hon. friend the Minister of Railways who is operating it, or my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham), it is a political affair, and you cannot get away from it. The present operation of the Intercolonial is a political operation, and as long as it is run as a government road I am afraid it will be a political operation.

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Not necessarily.

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
My hon. friend says
"not necessarily." Well, there must be a great regeneration in the minds of the people of Canada if you can run a government railway without having it a political affair. I think my hon. friends opposite will pretty nearly agree that what I am saying is correct.

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: If my hon. friend from Pietou (Mr. Macdonald) had charge of it, he would run it as a non-political railway.

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Possibly he would, but
he is an outstanding exception. Ordinary people obey the ordinary laws of humanity. You can talk all afternoon showing wherein you can get things done under the Railway Board on the Intercolonial, which you cannot get done at the present time. I know many people in the Martime Provinces fear that there may be an increase

in freight rates if the road is placed under the control of the Railway Board. I would be very sorry indeed to see such a result, but we must realize that Canada is facing the most serious financial condition she ever dreamed of, and if the Government is going to run a public utility it must be run on business principles. It must 'be made to pay, if it is night and proper it should pay. While I would be sorry to see an increase in freight rates, still if it is necessary in order that the road may be run as a business proposition, the Tates should be increased. Those are things we have to face, and I am getting old enough that I would like to see these utilities run on a business basis, so long as they are going to take the place of utilities that ought to be run on a business basis.
The press has been paying some attention to me in the last few days in connection with my views on public ownership, and I rather feel like reiterating them. My hon. friend the Minister of Railways may be a good business man, but he cannot run a railroad, as a government railroad. I think if he were president of a company railroad, and were running it as a business proposition, I would have about a6 much confidence in him as in any man I know, but he is not big enough to control the politicians, and he is not big enough to give the service we should have on the Intercolonial. Compare the service on the Intercolonial with the service on the Canadian Pacific, and you will wonder if both roads are in the same country. If a man starts out on a journey on the Intercolonial he allows twenty-four hours leeway. If he wants to be in Montreal on a ertain day, he is pretty sure of being there at the same hour the day following, whereas if he travels by the Canadian Pacific railway he is safe with fifteen or twenty minutes leeway.

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: That is all nonsense.

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
No, it is not nonsense. I know what I am talking about. I travel by the Canadian Pacific railway once a week, and I travel by the Intercolonial about once every three months. I have never travelled over the Intercolonial in the last ten years that I have not registered a vow of " never again." I have broken my vow, but I always register it. This condition of affairs is not the fault of the minister. It is the fault of the system. It is the fault of government ownership, or government operation. If you can get the Intercolonial established on a business
basis in certain things, and get certain rights from the Railway Board, it might have a rejuvenating effect on other portions of the railway. For those reasons, I am in favour of the proposition, except I think the minister should place the rights of suit against the railway under the ordinary law of the land, and treat the Intercolonial as an ordinary public utility, subject to all the laws and obligations of the country; and if it trespasses upon a man's rights he should be entitled to go before the ordinary courts of justice to obtain redress, just as he would do if he were dealing with the Canadian Pacific railway or any other private corporation.

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
It must be admitted that the Intercolonial occupies a unique position among the railways of Canada. It was-built as part and parcel of the Confederation arrangement. The Intercolonial railway has had many difficulties to overcome, and! if the road had been' built merely for commercial purposes, probably a very different route would have been followed. For various reasons they were obliged to follow the route they did in OTder to overcome natural obstacles, to fulfil political considerations, and to complete the bargain that had been arrived at in the Maritime Provinces. I have heard it contended in this House on many occasions that the Intercolonial railway, the Post Office Department, and various other branches of the public service which are operated by the Government for the benefit of the public, should not be operated merely for the purpose of making money. The Intercolonial' railway is not in the position of an ordinary private company with dividends to pay. The Intercolonial is serving a great public purpose along a route where a private company would have been very loath and very slow to build a line. The road is subject to water competition over practically its whole length. We are told that it was built in that way because the Imperial Government requirements had made it necessary that it should be close to the water. However, that is a remote question at the moment. About twenty-five miles of my constituency is served by the Intercolonial. I know if anything is sent direct to Halifax or St. John the same rate prevails on the Intercolonial as on the Canadian Pacific railway, but in what position would the people residing between the terminal noints be, following the change now contemplated? Will the rates be reduced, or will they be increased? Every one
43*

admits the fact that the creation of the Railway Board of Canada was a boon to the public. At the time this board was organized it was said by the Hon. Mr. Blair, then Minister of Railways, that any man in Canada could send a postcard to the board and secure justice from it. Personally, I believe the board has done immense service to the public. I would like to know from the minister if this change will confer any advantage on the people of Bonaven-ture county, for instance, who have no other railway but the Intercolonial?

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: All I can say is that the rates will be subject to the Railway Board. They cannot be raised without the consent of the board. I hope and trust they will not be lowered, because we would like to get something for running the road.

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Are the rates now in effect on the Inter colonial railway in that district lower than they would be on a corresponding railway where there is competition?

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: The Intercolonial Railway rates are lower than they are on the regular railways.

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Is it proposed to have them increased as a result of this transfer to the Railway Board?

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: That would depend on the Railway Board.

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Would the Governor in Council still have some control, and be able to take the peculiar situation of those communities into account, or will they be left to the tender mercies of the Railway Board?

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: The whole matter will be under the Railway Board, and that is the proper place for it.

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
It may as well be taken for granted that the result of this railway going under the Board of Railway Commissioners will be to Taise the rates. Notwithstanding all that has been said, there are many points on the Intercolonial where the rates are much lower than they would be under similar conditions on a company road where there is no competition. If you were to ask the manager of the road whether it is right or wrong to raise the rates, he will shut one eye and say: "We want it under the Board of Railway Commissioners because we will then get an increase in rates which will then be put on a par with the rates charged by private companies under similar circumstances. My hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvell) has talked about

sidings. He does not live on the Intercolonial.

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Yes, I do.

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: He lives on the Valley railway which is operated by the Intercolonial.

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: The Intercolonial has been brought within my county during the last two or three years and I have not seen any lowering of the rates. This talk about low rates on the Intercolonial under the Government is all moonshine.

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: There was no railway where the St. John Valley railway, operated by the Intercolonial, now is. That railway came in. At competitive points rates are the same but at non-competitive points the government railway rates have been less and those rates will be raised by the Board of Railway Commissioners because this railway will be put on exactly the same basis as -that occupied by a company railway. My hon. friend from Carle-ton is not living on the Intercolonial; he is on the St. John Valley railway and he has no sympathy with the old Intercolonial *as it was constructed for political and national purposes originally. He spoke of sidings. That made me smile. I smiled inwardly and outwardly at that. If he had been on the Intercolonial and if he had wanted a siding he would not have gone to the Board of Railway Commissioners and asked for siding on certain terms but he would have gone to the Government and asked for a siding for nothing. That is one of the difficulties of the government system. Hon. gentlemen will find this entering into their own experience. There are certain conditions under which railway companies -put in sidings. I think in all my experience I only found one man who wanted -to comply with the conditions when asking for a siding on the Intercolonial railway. They would urge that there were , special conditions under which the Government itself ought to build a siding and the men who ask for sidings do not want to make any contribution towards them. We had all these things to contend with. Under the Board of Railway Commissioners they will likely get an order for a siding but it will be on the terms that a railway company will get and that is that the gentleman making the application for the siding will have to pay a share of the cost.

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Certainly, why not?

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Why should he not?

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I am not saying that
he should not but I am pointing out that in ninety per cent of the cases in which applications are made for sidings, the people applying for the sidings are not wiling to be treated as they would be if they applied for a siding from a private Tailway company. What will happen if the application goes before the Railway Commissioners and the plea is made that the person making the application should not pay? If the Board of Railway Commissioners make an order a member need not go before the minister and say to him: Do not do this; you ought to pay for it, and my friend should not pay at all. He will have to do what the Board of Railway Commissioners order.

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: On a business basis.

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
On a businses basis. I am pointing out to my hon. friend from the Maritime Provinces what the Bill means. My hon. friend from Carleton does not appreciate what I am trying to get at. If he had been Minister of Railways for a number of years he would see the significance of what I am saying.
There is a clause of the Bill which strikes me as rather peculiar. While the Board of Railway Commissioners will be given the right to malke orders as to sidings, service and that kind of thing, it has no power to enforce its ruling and that is expressly provided for in the Bill. Section 4 says:
Notwithstanding anything contained herein or in the Railway Act, His Majesty shall not nor shall the Minister of Railways and Canals be liable to any fine or penalty, nor shall the board have power to impose any fine or penalty on His Majesty or on the Minister of Railways and Canals, and no order or judgment of the Board under or in consequence of which His Majesty would have to pay or expend any money shall have any force or effect until it has been approved by the Governor in Council.
That is the anomaly of putting the government railway under the Board. It cannot impose any penalty. The Canadian Pacific railway running side by side, .say, at some point, can be fined, a penalty can be imposed upon it, if it does not comply with the order of the board. But owing to the very condition of things His Majesty cannot be fined by the Board of Railway Commissioners. Unless there be some amendment by which the railway itself is divorced from His Majesty for practical purposes and can be compelled by the board to carry out its order, this Act may not amount to much.

speechtext:
Could the minister
be ordered by the board to do something and not carry out the order?

speechtext: That is what will happen. It may he an order that express No. 1 or No. 2 need not stop at a certain station. That is always a vexed question, you know. Suppose the board makes an order excusing an express from stopping and several prominent men in the community affected come to the minister and say: Notwithstanding what the board says, you must not carry out that order. The board is helpless to compel the railway to carry out its order. The minister may say: We will not do it. There is nothing to compel him to do it. That brings the decision of the Railway Board right hack to the minister again. Would it not be possible to ppt the findings of the Board of Railway Commissioners in the same category as the small claims, under the Small Claims Act, under which penalties may be imposed on the railway itself up to a certain amount for not carrying out the orders of the board? It seems anomalous but if something of that kind be not done you cannot carry out the orders of the board.

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Where would the money go that you would collect?

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.

speechtext: I presume so.

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Out of which it came?

It does not make any difference. I say that doing it at all is an anomaly. But by this Bill you give the board power to make orders and then you say it shall have no power to enforce those orders. It may be impossible to do it in any other way with a government railway but it only adds to the peculiarity of the situation created by the fact that the Government is really divesting itself of control and handing it over to a number of men appointed by itself to report to itself. It makes the situation anomalous. Unless there be some provision by which the

management itself can be compelled to carry out the orders of the board, notwithstanding this Act, the management will revert back to the minister and he will have to decide, just as he does at the present time, all questions* with reference to the operation of the road.	*

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Let me put a question to the hon. the ex-Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham). Would my hon. friend prefer to increase the rates, make money andi have a big surplus, or would he rather give the people reasonable rates?

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I think if the Intercolonial railway charged a sufficient rate to pay all its expenses and carrying charges, everybody would be satisfied.

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.

The illustration given by the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) with reference to sidings is one of the very forcible reasons which caused me to favour

this legislation, because no one can dispute that if .a private individual applied for a siding and through political influence oould get that siding for nothing, that would be at the expense of the whole community and it is something that should not be tolerated.

The Railway Board now in fixing rates do not consider whether there is competition, but they make a rate proportionate to the distance, just as if there were one thousand competitors. subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.

speechtext: I venture to say we give a good deal more traffic in proportion.

speechtext: You have more railway competition too.

speechtext: And it is according to the proportion of traffic given that the rates should be fixed.

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: My hon. friend forgets that central Canada gets all its freight carried on the canals absolutely free.

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I am not going into that political question at all. I do not care if they do make charge for the canals. No charge is made for our canals because they are in competition with the American canals and with the American railways.

speechtext: Ontario gets the benefit.

speechtext: We do- not get any special benefit. If you ship anything to the West by water you get the same benefit as we do. There is no use talking about that sort of sectional questions. speechtext: What remedy have the people?

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I wish he would consider that carefully. I feel so strongly on it that I would be prepared to dTaft an amendment.

speechtext:
Some of us who have lived along the Intercolonial all our lives think that we know a little more atoout conditions on the Intercolonial than our friend from North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt), or our friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvell). I say that with all deference to them.
4 p.m. My hon. friend from Carleton has in his district a hybrid railway called the St. John Valley railway, which is distinguished for the amount of money .that has been stolen in connection with it by Conservative politicians in New Brunswick, rather than for the amount of traffic carried on it. He has such an aversion to that road that I have no doubt he is biased against government operation of railways.
Some people who talk about the Intercolonial have forgotten that the Maritime Provinces are 'separated from the rest of Canada by a very narrow strip of territory, not more than 100 miles wide, stretching from the St. Lawrence to the state of Maine, and that the conditions under which Confederation was brought about 50 years ago were such that every student knows that it would not have been possible tout for the construction of the Intercolonial railway and for the assurance that the people of these provinces always had and which has
been maintained from that time uninterruptedly until the present time that on account of our isolation we were entitled to certain concessions and rights and privileges which do not obtain here in central Canada.
The Grand Trunk railway and various canals were established in central Canada long before there was a line of railway in the Maritime Provinces. Then came the Canadian Pacific railway, with its marvellous developments; and subsequently the network of railways that to-day runs through Quebec and Ontario. The only means of getting in and out of our province is through the thin line that runs along the south shore of the St. Lawrence from Levis east, along the north shore of New Brunswick to Moncton andi thence into Nova Scotia. Notwithstanding the conditions with regard to the size and population of that country, the Government propose to put the Intercolonial railway, in Tegard to freights and matters of that kind, upon the same plane as lines running through largely populated portions of Canada. My hor. friend is discriminating against that part of Canada, and disregarding the terms of Confederation. The member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) asked if the local Tates on the Intercolonial were lower than the rate9 in other parts of Canada. The minister said that they were. Does the minister want a board that he can use when he wants to put additional imposts upon the people of the Maritime provinces and whose rulings he need not obey if he does not want to? That is what he is doing here. If he wants to create company ownership of this road so that extensions may he made by companies interested in the development of our province, let him make a proposal to that effect. Notwithstanding what hon. gentlemen of this committee may say about the minister, -he is Tunning the Intercolonial under a system of patronage, consulting his political friends in every county; and he is going to do it when he gets this legislation through just as he did before. The minister dare not rise in his place and deny that assertion.

The superintendents of the divisions, when they want to employ men in any capacity, go to the gentlemen who have the patronage. It is true that the minister himself does not consult them, but his understrappers and officials have full instructions to do so. When a brake-man or trackman is to be employed the minister in Ottawa may not take the steps to which I refer, but the superintendents take the recommendation of the men who have the patronage. My hon. friend himself may be all right; but he knows that orders have gone forth in this regard, and that they are obeyed in respect of appointments that are made. If the minister wants to deal with this matter fairly, let him wipe out entirely the sysTem of patronage. If he is going to raise the rate of freight to the people of the Maritime Provinces, let him deal with the whole matter; let us not have the railway run by one

political party, in the interest of that party, without regard to the terms of Confederation, to the proper considerations involved in the question of rates, and to the isolation of our part of the country. I do not speak in a sectional way about this matter. Elon. gentlemen from Central Canada and the West forget that this thin line of territory of one hundred miles is the only territory binding the Maritime Provinces to the rest of the Dominion, through the medium of this one railway. No matter how we may develop our resources doyn there, if we look for a home market-as we all naturally do look-when we sell our products we can ship them to other parts of Canada only over this one line of railway. At the same time, we purchase manufactured goods from that part of Canada where such goods are manufactured, and we have to pay the impost which is made upon	us in respect of	the longhaul	necessary to reach	our	faraway part of the country. There can be only one purpose in the bringing up of this matter: that of increasing the rates. That might as well be definitely understood. My hon. friend is going to give to the commission power to do certain things-to increase the rates, forsooth-but if the railway causes the destruction by fire of 'the property of a man who lives along the railway line, the minister will say to him: It is true that the operation of the railway is now under the Railway Commission, but when it comes to our destroying your property, we are not going to give to you the same remedies that are obtainable by persons living in other parts of Canada. You cannot sue us without coming to the Exchequer Court and getting a fiat. And this notwithstanding the fact that a man who lives along the line of the Grand Trunk or the Canadian Pacific railway can immediately proceed in any court in event oi damage occurring or an accident taking place. My hon. friend is not fair in that. He should accede to the request of the member for Carleton and, if the object of this proposal is to increase the rates, give to the people the same remedies that the people in other parts of the country have when they are dealing with a company railway. Under the legislation introduced by the member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) when he was Minister of Railways, in the case of the killing of animals, the causing of fires or the occurrence of accidents, in respect of which the damages do not exceed $500, the matter can be adjudicated-

speechtext: It was only $200 when I came in.

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: When the man who suffers damage to the extent of $500 is able to obtain remedy in his local courts, why should the man whose damage exceeds $3,000 be obliged to proceed in the Exchequer Court? If that man lived in any other part of Canada he could get remedy in a local court. My hon. friend must admit that that is not a fair position for him to take. Some remedy for that ought to be found in this Bill. For myself, I would like to see patronage, no matter what party might be in power, absolutely done away with in all the public services of the Dominion. Party patronage is a disease that is sapping at the vitals of this country in regard to every dollar that is being expended for war or other purposes, and it ought to be wiped out. If the result of this measure would be in any way to bring about that end, it would have my fullest accord, even if it did involve extra expenditure to the province from which I come. But if we are simply to have the extra expense and at the same time the burden together with inconveniences which people in other parts of the country do not have-

speechtext: People in any part of the country in which the Government expropriates property have, if matters cannot be amicably adjusted, to come to Ottawa to have their claims disposed of.

I am not dealing with the question of expropriation of property: I am dealing with the question of a railway inflicting damage upon a man's property. If a railway in central Canada damages a man's property, that man can have his remedy in the local court. That is not the case with us, and it is a hardship for the people living in remote parts of the Dominion to have to bring their cases into the Exchequer Court.
We hear the cry:	Why should not the
people along the Intercolonial railway pay the same rates as other people do? I am not speaking in any sectional way, but before larger questions occupied the arena of this country, it was one of the [DOT] favourite occupations of certain of the press of Ontario to discuss seriously making the people who live along the Intercolonial railway pay higher rates. They forgot altogether that exactly the same sum of money as was spent on the Intercolonial Tailway was spent by the Dominion in the construction of the canal system, which was their means of transportation, and for the use
of which not a dollar is asked from the businessman who transports his goods along those canals.

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: The use of those canals in 'bringing goods from the Northwest down to the lower provinces lowers the freight to you.

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: We are dealing with a population in my province of 500,000 and with ,a population of about two millions in Quebec. The 'minister apparently thinks everything that is transported along the canals goes down into our province.

speechtext: No.

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: The transportation of goods on the canals does not involve in any considerable degree the carrying of goods to the Maritime Provinces, because of the extra cost of the second handling. No goods come to our country by sea; the goods that come to our country aTe carried by rail.

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Does the hon. member not realize that the mere fact that the existence of the canals reduces the freight rates on the railways, inures to the benefit of the people in the Maritime Provinces?

speechtext: My hon. friend is very solicitous for the people of the Maritime Provinces.

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I am not a bit solicitous; it is my hon. friend who is solicitous.

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: The freight rates on the railways of central Canada are fixed by the Board of Railway Commissioners, and according to the minister the rates fixed by that board are higher than the rates charged on the 'Intercolonial. I am not complaining aJbout the fact that the canals are carrying this freight. I am glad to see that those great waterways provide means for the transportation of the products of the country. What I complain of is the talk of those gentlemen who occasionally feel it their b'ounden duty to tell us in the Maritime Provinces: You must pay more.

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: We do not say so.

That has been said in this House, and it has been stated in the press of the country for the last fifteen years. If the minister is going to deal with this proposition, of what use is it submitting a Bill to Parliament which says: We are going to refer certain matters set out in the schedule to the Board of Railway Commissioners, tout if we do not like to

obey that board <we need not do so. That is what my hon. friend says, because that is the meaning of this section 4:
4. Notwithstanding anything contained herein or in the Railway Act, His Majesty shall not nor shall the Minister of Railways and Canals 'he liable to any fine or penalty, nor. shall the Board have power to impose any fine or penalty on His Majesty or on the Minister of Railways and Canals, and no order or judgment of the Board under or in consequence of which His Majesty would have to pay or expend any money shall have any force or effect until it has been approved by the Governor in Council.
The result is that you are under the hoard and you are not under the board. If the Government are not satisfied with an order made by the board, the Government need not -pay any attention to it. If the Government want to resort to the board as a cover to enable them to get something done, they can say to the people: Oh, the board ordered us to do that.

speechtext: We would hear from the hon. member in this House if we did not obey the decisions of the board.

The minister will
not find that I will attack him if he will obey "the decision of the board.
Mr. COCHRAiNE: They will certainly be obeyed so long as I am Minister of Railways.

speechtext:
Then why does the minister insert the section which expressly provides 'that the .board need' not be obeyed? All I plead for in connection with this matter-and I do not put it on sectional lines-iis this:	That our friends in other
parts of Canada should remember the conditions under which our Maritime Provinces are. We Ibuv our goods in central Canada and there is this long haul. Our maritime position would enable us to go to the United States seaboard for the purchase of goods, but the Intercolonial railway was created for the purpose of developing interprovincial trade and it has done so. For years the complaint was made that there was no return, traffic from the East to the West and that our industries and conditions in the Maritime Provinces did not give to the Intercolonial that return which would enable it to earn a profit. As we have gone along developing all our industries, our products have reached a stage which enables us to furnish to the Intercolonial a very large and increasing traffic. The minister now says that the rates aTe lower in the Maritime Provinces. I say: They have a right to he lower on account

of the isolation. That is all I plead for. I do not complain about anything concerning other parts of Canada, or about the people in any other part getting fair consideration. Numerically, we are small, and we are isolated on account of this narrow strip of territory through which we must go to get East or West. But do not let us in this Parliament approach the consideration of this question from this standpoint: Oh, the Intercolonial railway has been getting along with less freight than obtains in any other part of the country and the people should be compelled to pay higher rates.
The primary need of this railway is to give a service to the people living along the line, and by reason of the fact that this railway was constructed under the terms of Confederation, there was, by the express representation made by the public men of that day, guaranteed to the people of the Maritime provinces special considerations in regard to freight rates which should not be taken away. I do not give my hon. friend credit for being actuated by the sentiments I have mentioned as existing in certain parts, but do not let us approach this measure from the standpoint that the Tates should be raised.

speechtext: I did not say that.

Let there be no discrimination against the people of the Maritime Provinces by compelling them .to go to the Exchequer Court to have their claims .settled, whereas men in central Canada can have their claims settled in the provincial courts.	That is all I say
in regard to this matter, and a Bill of this kind, which does not deal with the whole question is quite inadequate. As I said iu my opening remarks the people of the Maritime Provinces ought to have been consulted on this question and their views taken into consideration before the minister introduced this legislation.

As a member of the Railway Committee, I am surprised at the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) taking the position he has taken in regard to this measure. There should be no question about the importance of bringing them under the Railway Commission, and I am sure the people of Canada will heartily approve the

action taken by the minister in that regard. The hon. gentleman from Pictou calls attention to the fact that the people in the Maritime Provinces have not had sufficient notice of this matter. It is some four months since the Minister of Railways stated that the Intercolonial would be [DOT]brought under the Railway Commission. The question has been pretty thoroughly discussed in the papers, in the House, and in the provinces, and general approval has been given to this measure. In addition to that, I am sure, if the hon. member from Pictou will inquire of the workmen along the Intercolonial, or along any of the Government railways, he will find the different organizations heartily approve of this measure, and I am sure the more he investigates this matter, the more satisfied he will become that the workmen and employees on the Government railways are heartily in favour of the roads being brought under the Railway Commission. The hon. gentleman must also know that the clauses in the Railway Act which deal with the questions affecting the employees on government railways will come under the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission.

There would be no sense in a government railway under the circumstances under which the Intercolonial has been built charging a rate of freight that would produce a surplus revenue to the railway. Surely, until we have the privilege that the people along the Intercolonial enjoy, we should not be subjected to an increase in freight rates. When we come to the seventh section of this Bill I


want to move an amendment to that effect, and I think it ought to appeal to the good sense of the members of the committee.
I regret to find that when matters of this kind are discussed, the members from Ontario seem to- think that the Intercolonial is operated altogether in the interest of the Maritime Provinces. They appear to tfiink that if there is no surplus from the road the Maritime Provinces get the benefit of it and that it is to the disadvantage of the rest of Canada and particularly of Ontario. That is the worst kind of a misapprehension. The Intercolonial is operated just as much for the advantage of the people of Ontario as of the Maritime Provinces. It is a link that binds Ontario and the Maritime Provinces together. The advantage is on the side of Ontario. We do not ship anything like the quantity of goods to Ontario that we get from that province. In the last few years the trade has been increasing and I am .very pleased. It is to the advantage of the whole country that the rates on the Intercolonial should be kept at the lowest possible point. This should be encouraged by members from every province and particularly from Ontario. The people of Ontario may not always have the high customs tariff which they enjoy to-day. There is growing up in this country a very strong sentiment that the manufacturers of Ontario have too many advantages now. The West will be heard from and the Maritime Provinces feel that they have paid tribute to the manufacturers of Ontario for a long time. The manufacturers of Ontario should be careful lest this spirit be developed and their privileges be reduced. One way to prevent this reduction is to continue the rates on the Intercolonial at the very lowest possible point.

Hughes) and who is just going out of the Chamber, but I do not expect him to substantiate what he says because he gets all mixed up. The next is the provision governing telegraphs and telephones. That is very important. I have some small interest in a telephone company in New

Brunswick, of which I am one of the directors. We have to do business with the Intercolonial railway; why should not the Railway Board of Canada be the arbiter between our company and the minister's company, just the same as it is between our company and the Canadian Pacific Railway company? I am pointing out what the omissions are. The next is the provision relating to1 marine electric telegraphs or cables. Then there is the provision with regard to Government use and construction of telegraphs and telephones. Then there is the matter , of statistics. Why should not the Intercolonial railway make returns of statistics to the board just the same as any other company does? That is section 380.
I now come to another phase of the matter. Section '4 of this Bill provides:
Notwithstanding anything contained herein or in the Railway Act, His Majesty shall not nor shall the Minister of Railways and Canals he liable to any fine or penalty, nor shall the Board have power to impose any fine or penalty on His Majesty or on the Minister of Railways and Canals, and no .order or judgment of the Board under or in consequence of which His Majesty would have to pay or expend any money shall have any force or effect until it has been approved by the Governor in Council.
I agree that the Minister of Railways should not be liable to fine or penalty; nobody would assume that the ministR would maliciously do anything for which he should be fined. But the latter part of this section absolutely takes away from the board the power of enforcing a decision by fine, penalty or imprisonment unless that decision is accepted by the Governor in Council. Whatever the board may do, therefore, is only a polite invitation to the Intercolonial Railway authorities that, in their judgment, certain things should be done. If the minister says no, then you cannot fine him; you cannot fine the Government; you cannot fine His Majesty. According to this Bill you cannot make the Intercolonial pay any money unless the Governor in Council says that it shall be paid.

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Does it not stand to reason that nothing is accomplished by putting money from one pocket into another?

subtopic: SECOND READING AND CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
No manager of the Intercolonial Railway Company wants to have his revenues reduced. If you make him pay the fine out of the railway moneys, he will try to run things so that he will not be obliged to pay. If his company is not subject to fines and penalties the manager will be just as independent as he has been during the last forty-five years. I admit that so far as the balance sheet of Canada is concerned, that would not make much difference; but it would make a wonderful difference in the work of the officers who are carrying on the affairs of the Intercolonial railway. Section 381 of the amended Railway Act is as follows:
Any company, or any director or officer thereof, or any receiver, trustee, lessee, agent, or person, acting for or employed by such [DOT] company, that does, causes or permits to be done, any matter, act or thing contrary to the provisions of this or the Special Act, or to the orders, regulations or directions of the Governor in Council, or of the minister, or of the Board, made under this Act, or omits to do any matter, act or thing, thereby required to be done on the part of any such company, or person, shall, in addition to being liable to any penalty elsewhere provided, be liable to any person injured by any such act or omission for the full amount of damages sustained thereby, and such damages shall not be subject to any special limitation except as expressly provided for by this or any other Act.
That provision is left out of the Bill now under consideration; therefore there is no such recourse against officers of the company as there is against the directors of a company railway. If my hon. friend wants to make this a railway company in the ordinary sense of the term, then the officials ought to be subject to the ordinary laws of the land.
The next clause that is left out is 387, which provides as follows:
All actions or suits for indemnity for any damages or injury sustained by reason of the construction or operation of the railway shall, and, notwithstanding anything in any special Act, may be commenced within two years next after the time when such supposed damage is sustained, etc.
That is the section which provides for bringing actions against a railway company. (1) Every railway company which fails or neglects to cause the thistles and all noxious weeds growing on the right of way, and upon land of the company adjoining the railway, to be cut down, or to be rooted Out and destroyed, each year, before such thistles or weeds have sufficiently matured to seed, or which fails or neglects to do anything which it is required by law to dq for the purpose of cutting down, or rooting out and destroying such thistles and weeds before they have sufficiently matured to seed, shall incur a penalty of two dollars for every day during which such failure or neglect continues.

(1) If any company refuses or neglects to comply with any order of the Board, made upon the report of the inspecting engineer, under the authority of this Act,-

speechtext:
The Intercolonial performs a service in many respects very much better than that given by the Canadian Pacific, or the Grand Trunk, in many other sections of Canada. However, will this Bill take the road out of politics? After all, that is the question. I do not think it possibly can have that effect. What was the purpose of establishing the Railway Board? It was created by Parliament to interpose between railway corporations and the public, to determine what was fair, as between the railway performing the service and the public receiving the service. It was quite natural and logical, therefore, that such a body should be established to regulate and control private railway companies, but does that principle apply to government-owned railways? These gov-

eminent railways are owned by the people, administered by the people, and the service is performed for the people. Therefore, this board is not intervening between any different interests. They are exercising control over a public utility which is owned by the people and carried on by the people. I do not think the placing of the Intercolonial under the jurisdiction of the Railway Board will assist in removing political influences from the administration of the road. I quite agree with hon. gentlemen this afternoon who object to political interference in connection with the administration of the government railway. We should endeavour to get away from it. We are likely to acquire the Canadian Northern Railway. Later on we probably will be obliged to take over the Grand Trunk Pacific, and it would appear to be desirable and necessary that some scheme be worked out for the administration of these two railways, and the Intercolonial railway, freed from political interference and political influence.
I was going to suggest to the minister that it would be as well to allow this matter to stand until we have disposed of the major railway problem of this country. The acquisition of the Canadian Northern is now before us. Next year we will probably have to deal with the acquisition of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and then will arise the question of the administration of these two Toads and the Intercolonial, and I trust some method may be evolved whereby they will be operated jointly free from partisan influence. It seems to me the only purpose to be served by this Bill will be the fixing and controlling of rates by the Railway Board. According to the statement of the hon. member (Mr. Carvell), a great many matters which are ordinarily within the jurisdiction of the Railway Board will be wanting in this case, and the powers which are sought to be placed in the Railway Board by this Bill practically refer only to the control of rates. The administration of the Intercolonial railway is somewhat different from the administration of other railways in Canada. Other railway systems extend from ocean to ocean. The Intercolonial is, relatively, a short road. Many problems confront the administration of the Intercolonial which are not found in other railways. This legislation seems anomalous, because you seek to introduce into the administration of the government railway another body created by the people, who own and operate the railway. Inasmuch as the Bill does not put the Intercolonial en-
tirely within the jurisdiction of the Railway Board, I would suggest that consideration of this matter might be postponed. I quite appreciate the desire of the minister to remove partisanship from the administration of the Intercolonial, and I sympathize with him in his efforts in that direction. At the same time I think we might well let the whole matter stand until we can deal thoroughly and effectively with our other railway problems.

Inasmuch as this Bill, if adopted, brings about such a radical change in the operation of the Intercolonial railway, it is natural that members from the Maritime Provinces, through whose constituencies the Intercolonial operates, should consider it carefully and find out why this radical change is being brought about at the present time. So far as I have been able to gather from the discussion this afternoon, there has not been one solitary reason advanced to show what advantage the Government, the country, or the Intercolonial railway will derive from the change the minister seeks to make. The only argument my hon. friend from Carleton advanced in favour of the Bill was that he had made a vow he would never travel on the Intercolonial again. So far as I can see, that is the only cogent argument offered in favour of the Bill.
I might say to my hon. friend from Carleton, without making a criticism of the argument he used, that I never would travel by the Canadian Pacific railway. This would not be an argument against the condition of that road. If my hon. friend wanted to make an argument in favour of the Canadian Pacific railway in comparison with the Intercolonial, I might make the same answer, but it is no argument why we should have this very radical change imposed upon us that the Intercolonial does not happen to be the line on which he travels. If the Intercolonial traversed the country through which my hon. friend travels, as the Canadian Pacific railway does, I venture to say that he would gladly accept the privilege of travelling over the Intercolonial. Many arguments against and criticisms of the Intercolonial are made, but I wish to say, on the other hand, that the Intercolonial has served a splendid purpose. It has served the people of the Maritime Provinces well, and it is a good railway. While it is true that, in the past, some political interfer- . enc-e may have taken place, while it may be true of the future and while it may be that the life of the Minister of Railways for the time being may not be the most pleasant in the world, still I am sure that my hon. friend the Minister of Railways (Mr. Cochrane) will not soon forget many pleasant excursions he has made oveT the Intercolonial, barring the one or two unpleasant receptions he had at Moncton. But the minister in going over the Intercolonial will see evidence on every hand that the Intercolonial is serving a splendid purpose, that it is traversing a good country and giving the people of the Maritime Provinces a valuable service. If so, I would like to ask the minister what demand has been made upon him by the people of the

Maritime Provinces or elsewhere to place the Intercolonial under the Board of Railway 'Commissioners. My hon. friend from Carleton says that all you will have to do will be to drop a postal note or send a telegram to the Chairman of the Board of Railway Commisioners and your grievance, if you have such, will be redressed instanter. That has not been my experience with the board. I am prepared to grant that this board has proved' a useful purpose. But it takes time, just as it takes time to confer with the general manager or the officials of the Intercolonial, to get matters adjusted or arranged. I have taken up matters with the Board of Railway Commissioners, and I have had to wait their pleasure to consider them and to make their findings. What is true of the Board of Railway Commissioners is true of the railway officials at Moncton.

There is a great deal of that going on. That is a small matter, I admit, but these are things that are increasing the cost of the operation of the Intercolonial Tailway and with this increasing cost it has been found necessary to increase the freight rates until the people who have to pay for the carriage of freight on the Intercolonial, particularly local freight, feel the burden severely. The minister will be well advised ilf he will take this matter into consideration, and, instead of increasing the freight rates on the Intercolonial, try to do something to reduce the expense of operation. speechtext:
