speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: THE CASCADE SCENIC RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I have made a cursory examination of the amendments, and they appear to me, .as .far as I can judge, to be in the public interest.
Motion agreed to.	,

Consideration resumed in committee of Bill No. 118, to amend the Government Railways Act.-Hon. Frank Cochrane-Mr. Rainville in the Chair.
On section 2-Definitions:

I beg to move that paragraph (b), section 2, be amended by inserting immediately after the word " railways," in line 9, the words " or 1 Canadian Government railways '," and by inserting immediately after the word " Canada," in line 13, the words " and operated under the control and management of the Minister of Railways and Canals."	.

Does the minister think that these words would be strong enough to cover the case of the Canadian Northern Railway system if the Bill which is now under consideration by the House in respect to that railway goes through? Personally, I think not. It would be a great mistake to bring the Canadian Northern Railway system under the control of this Act as it is now drafted.
This amendment is merely to make statutory recognition of the designation used in labelling rolling stock.
It is not intended, then, that the Canadian Northern railway will come under this Act if the Bill dealing with that railway is adopted?
I do not know. The Bill has not yet been adopted, and I cannot express an opinion.
It is a very important point.
Upon the passing of the Act a new board of directors would be appointed for the Canadian Northern Railway system, and it would he operated separately from the other government railways.

Subsection (b) of section 2 says:	.
"Government railways" means and includes all railways and all properties and works in connection therewith, owned, leased or in any way controlled by His Majesty in the right of his Government of the Dominion of Canada.
If the language were left as originally drafted, it might be contended that the Canadian Northern would come under the operations of the Bill. I apprehend that the minister by his amendment seeks to limit the operations of this Bill to such railways as His Majesty, through my hon. friend's department, regularly operates.
Yes.

Amendment agreed to, and section as amended agreed to.
On section 3-Application of certain sections of Railway Act to government railways :
In view of what I pointed out this afternoon-and of what I did not point out, at the request of the minister- I think this section ought to stand.
What objection do you take to this section?
This is the section that adopts the schedule; this section and the schedule should be considered together.
There would be no objection to coming back to this section if the schedule were not carried as my hon. friend thought proper.
Logically, this section ought to stand until we see what is in the schedule. If we pass this in advance, we are passing the schedule, the contents of which we do not know.

All right; let it stand.
Section stands.
On section 4-No fine or penalty to be imposed upon His Majesty or the minister!

This section is certainly objectionable. If the railway-I do not care what you call it, the minister or His Majesty or whatever it may be-is not liable to any fine or penalty under the Railway Act, we might as well throw this Bill into the waste basket, because if that be the 
case, the only object of this Bill is to give the board the power to increase the rates on the Intercolonial and not to give it power over anything else. I do not think that was the intention of the minister, and I know it was not the intention of the subcommittee that had Bill No. 13 under consideration. We went over this matter, and i't was the unanimous opinion of the Railway Committee that the government railways should be brought undeT the Railway Act. I am not trying to obstruct the passage of this Bill; I am trying to assist the minister to make it as workable as possible. If you say that this railway is going to be under the General Railway Act of Canada, and then say that is not subject to any orders of the board which mean the expenditure of money, or the payment of penalties or submission to fines, unless the matter first has the' approval of the Governor in Council, then all that you are doing goes for naught, the Railway Board has practically no power at all. The Railway Board can pass an order saying that, in their judgment, certain things ought to be, but if the Intercolonial Railway authorities do not want to obey that order, they need not do so.

I do not think any
minister could stand the pressure.

Then, let us have the
Bill so that we shall not have to stand the pressure. That is what we want. The minister has. been up against pressure ever since he has been in office, and every Minister of Railways has been up against pressure.
Surely the ho>n. member does not refer to me?

When my hon. friend
from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) was Minister of Railways, he was subject to just as much pressure as the present minister is, and just as long as it is possible for a politician to get after the minister, he will do so. I would like to see this Bill dtafted in such a way that there would be no possibility of a politician getting after the minister in any of these matters. Let us put the railway under the board so that the board will have some jurisdiction over it. The minister must admit that under section 4, if the board make an order, let us say. that certain appliances must be provided, as they have a right under the Railway Act to do, and say: If you do not do this thing, we will fine you; the Intercolonial railway authorities may say: It is true the Board jf

Railway Commissioners wish us to provide these appliances, but they have no power to enforce their order, they cannot punish us if we do not provide them. And some influential politician down in Moncton may say: I think if we enforce this, we shall lose votes. Therefore, it will not be enforced. This measure is the nakedest skeleton I have ever seen in my life-there is absolutely nothing to it whatever. I realize there might perhaps be a little incongruity in saying that a creation of the Crown shall have the power to fine the Crown and subject it to penalties. The difficulty is that this affects not only the Crown but all its officials. Secion 428 refers to carrying dangerous goods, and every company which does that, except in conformity with the regulations made by the board, shall be subject to a penalty of $500. But under this Bill, the Government railways can do as they please and nobody has a word to say about the matter. Section 429 provides that if any railway company improperly refuses to check baggage, they are subject to a penalty. That section is cut out of this Bill. I referred before to sections relating to making returns concerning accidents, refusal to make returns required by the board, and making false returns. Section 441, which should be discussed under this section, provides:
For the purpose of enforcing any penalty under any of the provisions of this Act, or enforcing any regulation, order, or direction of the Governor in Council, the minister, the Board, or any inspecting engineer, made under this Act, the act, omission, or failure of any officer, agent, or other person acting for, or employed hy the company, shall, if within the scope of his employment, in every case be also deemed to be the act, omission or failure of such company.
That is a very important provision of the Railway Act, but it does not apply to this Bill. Subsection 2 provides that the company is liable to the same penalty as an individual offender, but that is all cut out of this Bill, and neither the individual offender nor the company would be liable. There is a section, which I am not able to find at the moment, which provides that a railway company is liable for all acts or omissions of its officers. That section is not included in this Bill, so that any officer of the Intercolonial may be as negligent as he chooses, and the company assumes no responsibility.
If we take section by section, we shall get through the Bill.
I am doing so.
No, the hon. member is not.
I am just pointing out to the minister-
Yes, I am not objecting to that, but we are getting away from the subject.

I am on the subject; I am pointing out to the minister that if he leaves section 4 as it is, then all those sections providing for penalties are absolutely nugatory-they are eliminated from this Bill. I look upon section 4 as the most objectionable section of them all, and the minister should consider very carefully whether he wishes to force this section through, or whether he will not allow this Bill to stand and change the section in some way so that the provisions of the Railway Act will apply to the Intercolonial.

The hon. member has referred to the penalties imposed under this Bill on the company. That would mean His Majesty. Section 4 provides that no penalty shall be imposed on His Majesty. Therefore all such clauses are properly omitted. The imposition of penalties by summary proceedings would bring His Majesty into all the lower courts without a fiat.

If His Majesty is going to be a railway company, then His Majesty should be a railway company, and he should be subject to the laws of the land. That is what I am arguing. I do not know who has furnished that memorandum for my hon. friend, but it sounds to me as if it were furnished by the man who drafted the Bill. Why should not His Majesty, if he is to be a railway company, be subject to a penalty? If he is going to carry goods and run trains, and if he assumes all the privileges of a public utility corporation, why should he not assume all the responsibilities of it as well? I should like to see the government railways under the Railway Act, and I should like to see every section possible of the Railway Act made applicable to the operation of the Intercolonial.

Perhaps I appreciate as much as any person the difficulties of the situation. It took me a full year to get the Justice Department to consent to allowing men having claims for damages on the line to sue up to the amount of $200. There seems to be a sort of aristocracy in the Justice Department which sticks to the old saying, so far as railways are concerned, that the King can do no wrong. The King, if he is running a railway, can kill a cow just the same as if he were not a King, and

he ought to be subject to the same laws so far as possible as Lord Shaughnessy is when he is running a railway. We ought to get away from that bit of mythology about the non-liability of the King when he goes into private enterprises.
I understand the legal difficulties the department has in drawing up a Bill to put this railway under the jurisdiction of the Bailway Board, so long as the department insists that the King can do no wrong, even if he is running a railway. That is the proposition the Bailway Department finds itself up against. Would there be a violation of the constitution, or of the divine right of kings-when they are running railways-if we put a clause in the Act reading:	"For the purposes of this Act the
management of the Canadian Government railways shall stand in the same position as if it were a private company." The hon. gentleman from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) said: But the money would be paid 'by the King and would go back to His Majesty. Still there would be this difference, that there would be a penalty that the management of the railway would fear-it would increase the cost of running the railway to that extent. I think, if something of that kind were placed in the Act, it would remove the difficulty and would, in the eyes of the public at least, place this railway in the same position as if it were a company railway. Would the Minister of Justice tell us. what harm would be done it an amendment such as the one I suggested were placed in the Act, in legal-phrase?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That is a large question. What harm would be done would be difficult to say, but I think that what is asked for would be the complete revolution of a principle established and recognized in our form of government I fancy ever since it commenced, and probably much more absolute in the old days than it is to-day. It seems to me it would be a very incongruous thing to have His Majesty, even if he be running a railway, subject to -be summoned before the sort of tribunal that would be imposing a penalty. I understand that this is a question of imposing penalties. I do not know why there should be any difference made with regard to the running of a railway more than with regard to any other matter, where a claim is made against Crown. I do not know that there is any greater reason for not enforcing a claim because it is connected with railway operation than there would be with regard to any

similar claim resulting from the wrongdoing or negligence of an agent or employee of the Crown. The hon. gentleman asked me what harm would be done. Perhaps I might ask him, what great harm results from, applying to the Crown the responsibility for what might happen in connection with anything else? The same argument that would apply to the case of the ordinary railway would apply to the responsibility of the Crown. With regard to claims arising out of the operation of this railway, 'precisely the same recoiirse would be open to a claimant which is open with regard to any other claim for which the Crown may be legally responsible; that is to say, a petition of right is open to everybody. The hon. member referred to a difficulty in obtaining consent from the Department of Justice-which is apparently held responsible for this principle of law-to have proceedings taken in ordinary form for damages up to $200. That is certainly a departure from the general practice. I think there is a great deal to be said in 'favour of the proposition that the Crown, at all events as regards civil liability, should be liable to be sued as other people are .sued, without the formality of a petition of right. But, after all, I think that in actual practice the issue of a petition of right is, to-day at all events practically a formality; the cases in which petition of right is refused are certainly very few and very far between. I do not think there has been an instance fox a long time past of the refusal to grant a petition of right where, upon the face of the contention, there was any colourable right that could be enforced. I occasionally hear my predecessor in my present office express a very liberal view-may I call it?-.as to the manner in which these petitions should be granted, and I think, notwithstanding the change in the occupancy of the office, we have acted, in that regard in no less liberal manner. There is not any serious difficulty interposed in the way of any person who has a legal claim by this requirement, which is in accordance with what has been the rule and the law under our constitution from time immemorial-that there should be leave of the Crown in order that the Crown might be sued. As regards the civil liability resulting from the operation of the railway, that is the only obstacle that stands in the way of the enforcement of such legal liability. I aim not absolutely familiar with the provisions of this Bill, and I have not had occasion to deal with

it personally. I understand these provisions relieve the Crown from the responsibility for penalties simply.
That is it.

The minister has introduced a Bill to place the government railways under the Railway Commission. A private corporation running a railway must obey the orders of the board or be subject to penalty. This clause we are discussing will exempt the government railways from any fines or penalties; in other words, the Board of Railway Commissioners can order us to do something, but if we do not do it, there is no way of enforcing the order.
That is the point.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Is there any reason to apprehend that the Government, at whose instance this railway is placed, under the direction of the Board of Railway Commissioners, will fail to comply with the orders that are made? With reference to any ordinary judgment that is rendered against the Crown, there does not seem to be any reason to apprehend that it will not be satisfied. I do not know it is contemplated that they should proceed to seize the public property in satisfaction of a judgment. I think the general assumption is that where there is that direction, that the Crown shall act under the direction of any particular body, it will be complied with; but I know of no cases where there is provision for penalties being imposed upon the Crown for disobedience to directions so made. After all, is this anything more than taking the direction of the government railway, in regard to certain matters out of the hands of the Government and placing it in the hands of the Railway Board? Instead of the minister, or the Department of Justice, or the Government itself, deciding what shall be done, it will be decided by the Railway Board. After we have that decision it is for the Government to carry it out, just as it would carry out the decision of the minister or of the Government itself. I do not think the idea is to make it compulsory on the Government to do these things which are right, but to have the decision of the question of what is right for the Government to do in the carrying on of the railway operations left to the same board that decides what it is right for the railway company to do.
You get the two bodies acting under the direction of the same body. The only difference is that the railway companies generally are subject to compulsion to act,
whereas with regard to the administration of a government railway, as I understand it, you have the provision in effect that operations are to be carried on under the direction of the Railway Board. It seems to me it can hardly be assumed that the law providing for the direction of the operations of this railway, which is a government railway, shall be in the hands of the Railway Board, and that you must look to means of compulsion to be exercised upon the Government to carry out the direction of that body in whose hands the direction is placed by the law itself.

May I ask the minister
a question? The Railway Board being subservient to the Government, can the Railway Board order the Government, which is superior to it and which is its creator, to do an act which the Government may be unwilling to perform; and the Government, acting as His Majesty and being unable to do any wrong, can its servant, or His Majesty's servant, order His Majesty to perform an act against His Majesty's will?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That is precisely the
condition of affairs that my bon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) complains of. While there may be .something to be said for instituting a system where you submit His Majesty-that is the country to the same control and direction of courts or to a board of this kind as other people are subjected to, yet, until ith-e principles to which the hon. member for Wright (Mr. Devlin) has referred are departed from in our constitutional system, I do not think we can arrive at a situation where a body appointed by the Government shall be given power to exercise compulsion on the Government.
Mr. 'CARVELL: My hon. friend is facing the thing pretty well, I think, but he is forgetting the fact that Canada is branching out to-day on a very much extended application of the principle of public ownership and public operation of railroads. I would not say as much as I have said on this Bill were it not for the fact that another Bill is before Parliament by which the Government proposes to take over and operate one of the great transcontinental systems of Canada. I know there is a great idea in the country that the people can operate a public utility better than a corporation can. If you take that in the sense of .spending more money, multiplying officials, decreasing efficiency, and everything else that goes with government operation, I admit you may be cor-

rect. But if it means doing things on business principles, getting the best service you can out of your employees, and giving the cheapest and best service to the public, then everything that has taken place in the way of public ownership up to the present has been an absolute failure. I am trying to guard against that condition of affairs in the future, so far as the railway law is concerned. The minister says he is going to bring the Intercolonial under the control of the Railway Board. The road will then be in the same position as all other railway systems in Canada brought under government control and operation. My hon. friend says: " Can you give an instance of government-owned railways refusing to carry out the instructions or orders of the Railway Board? Of course we cannot, because they have never been under the Railway Board so far.
Has any private road been fined?
I don't know.
I do not think so.

I imagine if they have not it is because the law is there, and they know they will be fined. This club is held over their heads. My hon. friend asks: Can you conceive of a government refusing to obey the orders of the Railway Board? My answer is, I can conceive of it without any difficulty. I can conceive of an official failing to do what he should do, and some aggrieved patron of the road applying to the Railway Board and getting an order directing the railway to do a certain thing within a certain time. That is just where the politician will get in his work. You can quite understand that this may affect something political in the community, and the politician will go to the minister and say: Now, we are going to lose votes if this thing goes through; therefore it should not go through. It will be sent up to the council, and the council will be influenced by the same things as influenced the minister. Government officials are eternally shifting responsibility on to somebody else. I do not care who may be under the government control or in the government service, inside of six months he will be demanding more pay and less work. That is constitutional. I am not finding fault with any one official; it applies to the whole body of public officials-more pay and less work-that is the habit. You put a man in charge of a government railway, and

for some reason or other he gets it into his head that he must not meet the demands of the people, and he is always warding them off. He feels that the man who makes an innovation is interfering in some way with his dignity, and he shifts it off and says, No, you cannot do that. I never had but one constituent on the Intercolonial in my life. I was thankful when we went out of office. There was only one to - fire. They fired him, and I did not blame them. I could see a most wonderful change in that man inside of two years. When he went to the road he was a real active live wire; when he left it, he was a machine; his idea was-don't do anything-shift it up to the man next above-let it go on- get around your responsibility. If there was a penalty applicable to the railway, in the event of it failing to do its duty or carry out the instructions of the Board, these officials would become more like business men who run business corporations. Take the three great railways of Canada to-day, the Grand Trunk, the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian Northern; in my estimation you will find the best class of men Canada has ever produced in these companies-real live business men, who meet situations as they arise, men who make decisions, and see that those decisions are carried into effect. This is simply because the railway companies hold them responsible. The railway companies themselves are responsible for the carrying out of the directions of the board, and know full well that if they do not give the service, meet the wishes of the people, the Board of Railway Commissioners has power to compel them to do it. My contention is, if the Intercolonial were placed in the same position as a corporation is, then the railway company, as I choose to style it, will say to its employees: You must do business, and do it on business principles; if you do not, you are under the instructions of the board and you will be fined, or punished. The railway employee would then realize that he is part of this machine, and not a mere cog in the political wheel; he would appreciate the fact that he was there to help the railway, to exercise his thinking powers, and be a man of action. The country has to get service, which it does not get at the present time. After all it is a pyschological question, and it is from that point of view that I am opposed to public ownership and public operation. You never can get anything out of men who are simply government officials. They are merely waiting for four o'clock to come.

I am not blaming them at all, it is constitutional with them and they cannot help it. But surely, when we are passing laws affecting these people, we should try to frame our laws so as to get the best cut of them.
When this country is about to launch into a great system of Government operation, I do hope that we will try to get what we can out of it. It will be a pretty poor service, and it will cost almost twice as much as it will under present conditions, but if we are going to have it let us see that it is efficient when we are starting. But there is a much greater principle at stake than the mere fact of taking some money jut of the Crown, and that principle is that the men we have in charge of the Intercolonial shall have some spur to operate it as a business proposition. Bor that reason I contend that this clause 4 should be entirely changed; in fact, I think it should (be eliminated altogether. I can see no reason for it.
What harm would it be to leave it out?

Yes, and let the road be a real railway. If the King is going to run a railway, let him run it like any other man, and if he does not do it right let him pay the penalty. Why should we not extend this liability to the officials of the road and make them pay the penalty as well as the King? Ilf you do you will get efficiency which you will not get unless there is some such drastic provision contained in this Bill.

I understood from the minister that he was going to amend section 4 and that he only wanted to exempt the Government railways from liability to fine and expropriation. But section 4 exempts them from everything. I should like to see the minister go very much farther than apparently this Bill intends to go With reference to bringing the railway under the Railway Board. I join with my hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvell) in asking the minister to have this clause amended very materially.

I sympathize with the views of my hon. friend from Carleton, but I see great difficulties in the way of fining the King. My suggestion this afternoon as to that has not been satisfactorily answered. If you fine the King $500 it means that he pays the fine to himself and he is no worse off than before. It is probably a
little annoyance to be fined, but he is no worse off-^he has the money in the other pocket. I think there is something in the suggestion of the hon. member for Carleton about officials. Could we not fine the officials? This road is to toe run by officials. If the Railway Board makes an order that it is the duty of an officer before he malt^s a change in the tariff to file it with the board, and he neglects to comply with that ordeT, he should be made liable. If a railway company proposes to make a change in freight or passenger rates the new rates are to be filed so many days before they become effective and if the responsible official neglects to perform that duty and puts the rates in operation without filing the schedule he is fined. Why not deal with an official of the government railway in the same way? I think you would get somewhere if you decided to fine the officer of the railway if he refused to comply with the direction of the board. You would get farther than if you placed the fine on the King. No one suggests that we should put the King in jail if he refuses to pay, or that we should arrest the minister. I do not think there is anything to be gained by a step of that kind, but there is a great deal to be gained by fining the superintendent of that railway.
Mr, GRAHAM: The King will pay his fine.
No, he will not.

The section under
discussion is the fundamental section in regard to the whole Bill. While I personally do not agree with the principle of the Bill, I assume that we have passed that stage, and I would like to do what I can in the way of suggesting amendments to the minister so as to make this measure as workable as possible. Under section 4 the situation would be that practically any application made to the Board of Railway Commissioners would be nugatory if it were made by any other person than the Department of Railways and Canals itself. If the Railway Department choose to deal with a question, what will be the use following the provisions of the Act, of submitting it to the Board of Railway Commissioners without any certainty that the order made will go into effect? Suppose my hon. friend from Carleton, or myself, acting on behalf of a client who had some rights which he thought had been infringed by the Government-for instance, a right granted to him under any other clause of

the Railway Act-went to the Railway Commission and asked them to decide upon the matter. Suppose that the board decides in favour of our application. But when they had decided, action, so far as the individual would be concerned, would be barred and we should simply be 'back to the point at which we started.
It is simply the opinion of the boiard.

It :s simply the opinion of the board. It may be a very fair and interesting document, but in so far as getting any relief for the party interested is concerned, it has no value whatever. I am at ,a loss to know what the situation would be if this clause were adopted. I do not think it would be possible for a party who had made a complaint to the board to get any relief whatever. But the minister comes in with section 4 and absolutely bars the way. Although there are penalities prescribed by the Railway Act, penalties shall not be exacted of His Majesty, or the Minister of Railways and Canals. I do not think they could have been exacted any way, and therefore I think the section is pure surplusage. I do not think there is under the common law, such a thing as collecting from the Crown unless by express Act of Parliament. This section takes away a right that really does not exist in common law no matter what the judges may say. I apprehend that the minister wants the statute to be of some practical good. With reference to the difficulty that the minister speaks about in connection with proceeding against His Majesty. I remember the occasion when my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) then Minister of Railways and Canals, was /perfectly willing Ito accept enactment of the Small Claims Act, and I remember the greatest possible difficulties were suggested by Sir Allen Aylesworth, who was then Minister of Justice and who -with all the instincts of the great lawyer that he is-regarded with a sort of holy horror the idea of departing from the principle that when you are proceeding against the Crown you should proceed by petition of right. However, a system was inaugurated under which an ordinary party who desired to enforce a claim instead of being obliged under the law to go to the Exchequer Court, was permitted to proceed in the ordinary courts, not against His Majesty, but against the Government Railway Managing Board who are the parties who 
ought to be proceeded against. After all, ajs a matter of practical result, it is a pure fiction to speak of the Crown managing the Canadian Government railways. The persons who run the Canadian Government railways are the general manager and his officials, subject to the minister as a court of appeal. It is not to he assumed that the minister knows all the 'details of the operations which are carried on by the general manager. It is impossible to conceive that he would. The responsibility for the proper operation of the road in detail rests upon the man who has the confidence of the minister as general manager. The minister himself, in 1914, agreed that:
In any action, suit or other proceeding, His Majesty shall not he cited as defendant, but the process shall he issued against the General Manager of Government railways, and such process may be served on him or any other person duly authorized by him to accept such service of, or be served with, processes in such cases-
Why should not the minister insert in this Bill a provision that where any right to a penalty accrues by reason of failure to carry out the orders of the Board of Railway Commissioners, the party who would be liable, mutatis mutandis, as compared with the railway company, would be the General Manager of the Canadian Government railways, or of the particular railway against which the order was made? I suggest to the minister that the difficulty could be remedied by striking out this section and simply providing in a short section by apt words that the party who should be proceeded against with the idea of enforcing the orders of the board should be the general manager of the railway from time to time. My desire in suggesting that is that both ministers may agree that we are here faced by an anomalous situation. 1 apprehend that the present minister is anxious in placing the government railways under the control of the Board of Railway Commissioners, to place the people operating the railway in the same position as those operating the Canadian Pacific, the Canadian Northern or any other railway, otherwise it is a work of supererogation. Why, therefore, if it is intended that the railway in its operation is to be on the same basis as a company railway, should not the provisions of the Small Claims Act be adopted so that the General Manager of the Canadian Government railways or the manager of the particular railway against whom the order is made would be responsible for the carrying out of the order?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: So far as this section is concerned, it does not seem to prevent what the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) was contending ought to be done.
Every section by which the officer or agent could possibly be held responsible for anything has been eliminated from this Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. gentleman referred to the Small Claims provisions. In cases where parties take their recourse before the ordinary courts as against the Crown, I do not understand that the judgment does more than determine that the Crown ought to pay the money. I doubt if in any court there is provision under which, if the Government did not provide the money to pay a claim awarded by a court, any process would issue against His Majesty to execute that judgment. Then you are in the same position with regard to an order of the Railway Board as His Majesty is with regard to the judgment of a court.
Parliament could take any property of the Government or of His Majesty to satisfy a judgment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Parliament could if it chose to.
If a man sued His Majesty and got judgment for a small claim and His Majesty did not want to pay, how would you collect judgment?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If you got your judgment under this Small Claims provision I do not think there is any means of enforcing payment; but you have a determination that you are entitled to the money, just as here you will have from the Railway Board a determination that a certain thing ought to be done.
The effect of this Act is to put into the hands of the Railway Board the determination of how tie Intercolonial railway shall be carried on and dealt with in respect of matters coming before that Board. The effect of it is not to enable the Railway Board to exercise compulsion upon His Majesty-at all events, any further than a court exercises compulsion upon His Majesty when it says that a certain sum is a proper amount for His Majesty to pay.

Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention to discuss from a legal viewpoint the several clauses of the Bill under discussion, I will restrict my remarks to certain statements made by hon.
gentlemen on the other side, in the course of the discussion, concerning the administration of the Intercolonial railway and the supposed political partisanship of the Minister of Railways.
It is not my privilege to (be on the railway committee and so, I did not have the opportunity to study the Bill and much less to take part in the discussion before the committee. That is the reason why I am under the necessity of offering now those few remarks.
Hon. gentlemen from Ontario never let a session pass without raising protracted debates and indulging in recriminations against the administration of the Intercolonial railway. Should any hon. gentleman be expected to abstain from dealing with questions relating to the Intercolonial railway they are the hon. members coming from the province of Ontario, since that railway runs exclusively through Quebec and the Maritime Provinces. Yet, as I said before, at every session these hon. gentlemen are raising objections and complaining of the heavy expenditures incurred in the administration of the line. My hon. friends ought to keep in mind that we of the province of Quebec, do not begrudge them the expenditure in relation to the management of the canals or to the construction of a railway for which ithe country will probably never have any use-the Hudson Bay railway.
Neither do we begrudge them the millions upon millions spent by .this country upon the construction of railways in the West, the advantages of which have accrued to Ontario, in a much larger measure than to the province of Quebec. As I said before, it seems to me that it would only be fair that these gentlemen should put an end to their continuous wrangles over the Intercolonial.
We are told that it stands to reason that ' the western interests are altogether different from the eastern interests. If, since 1867 until now, that is to isay, after being confederated for fifty years, we have not been able to come to an understanding, then, should it not be best to part amicably?
I heard the hon. member from Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) say this .afternoon that the Intercolonial railway employees would be pleased to come under the railway commission. I do not know where he,got that information, but I think it is a wild statement, .because I know a numbeT of men upon that road-a great many personally -better than my hon. friend could know

them, and I am sure that such is not their opinion.
I ialso remember that my hon. friend said that we, the members from Quebec and the Maritime orovinces, ought not to fear any interference from the railway commission iso far as the rates are concerned, adding that we would toe well safeguarded against it. I shall take upon imyself to ask the hon. member from Lamtolton who are the representatives of Quebec and the Maritime provinces upon the railway commission. It is true we have the hon. Mr. Nantel, but after .ail he belongs to the western part of the province of Quebec, he is not at all familiar with the conditions prevailing in the eastern phrt of the province, and much less, in the Maritime provinces.
We are somewhat unfairly treated on that score. We should have .a representative upon the railway commission; it would only be fair. Among six representatives, we have but one who belongs Ito Quebec, but he comes from the western part of the province. Although there are three of them, the Maritime provinces are not represented upon the railway commission.
It seems that there is a discripiination in that respect. We cannot expect to get a fair treatment at the hands of people who are not familiar with our needs and who belong to another part of the Dominion of Canada.
The member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) this afternoon indulged in considerable criticism of the Intercolonial railway. He said that he preferred to travel by the Canadian Pacific. My hon. friend knows- because he has been in the House a good deal longer than I have-the conditions under which the Intercolonial is run. The Canadian Pacific runs a good deal further south, and across a country in uhich there is much less snow than in the country traversed by the Intercolonial. Consequently, it is not surprising that it sometimes makes better time in winter than the Intercolonial. The Intercolonial goes as far north as a railroad can go, and, having regard to the weather conditions in the country between Bathurst and Camp-bellton and Levis, it is sometimes difficult for the trains to run on time. But under favourable weather conditions, this road competes favourably with the Canadian Pacific. When we compare the time-tables of the two roads, we find that the advantage is with the Intercolonial. Of course, sometimes the trains are late because there being a good deal of traffic on the road and because of the fact that the Intercolonial 
tries to give the public as much accommodation as possible by stopping at places where, perhaps, the Canadian Pacific would not stop. I think that the Intercolonial runs about 35 miles an hour, while the Canadian Pacific runs about 32. Even though the trains are sometimes half an hour late in reaching Montreal, we should bear in mind the fact that the Intercolonial is our own road and that it should be encouraged in preference to the other. Some hon. gentlemen on the other side have said that political partisanship is practised in connection with the administration of the Intercolonial. Well, I know something about the administration of that road. During some years I have not been on the best of terms with the Minister of Railways; consequently my opinion should be accepted as that of a man well posted on matters connected with the administration of the railway. The difficulty between the Minister of Railways and myself occurred because he did not want to run the road from a partisan standpoint; he did not want to do what I wanted him to do.
That is an honest confession.

He did not want to follow exactly the methods followed by the Liberal party in 1896. I say that from an ifide-pendent point of view, and if I have become so independent since I have been in this House-because I was quite a Conservative when I became a member1-it is because the Minister of Railways has not been running his railway from a/partisan standpoint. Ilf there is any one who deserves praise for his . non-partisanship it is the Minister of Railways.
The minister is all right personally.

Let me give my hon. friend .an example of the w.ay in which the Liberal party used to treat us. One day during the political campaign of 1904 I was in a station on the Intercolonial. One of the railway employees had left his station and come down on a handcar to the next 3tati'on, at which I was, a distance of about fifteen miles. He amused himself for about half an hour in insulting me on the station platform, although I had my ticket in my pocket and was waiting for the train and was quite within my rights in being there. I reported the matter at the time to the Minister of Railways, who, of course, was a Liberal, and gave him all the facts. Did I receive any justice? No, No investigation

was held. The superintendent wished to have an investigation because he thought it was only fair for a citizen to have one so that he could prove his charge. The Minister of Railways, however, acting differently from what a minister should do, forbade an investigation, and I did not have an opportunity of proving what I had stated. The result was that the man was retained in his position, and, of course, he w.as encouraged, and the other employees were encouraged, to insult poor fellows who happened to be Conservatives. That was the way in which we were used during the Liberal administration, hut such a shameful thing has never happened on the Intercolonial since 1911.
We axe satisfied with the administration of the Intercolonial. We do not expect it to do any better under the circumstances under which that road is run, and we do not wish any change. If I have said in this House anything against the administration it has not ibeen against the w,ay in which the road is administered, but it has always been in connection with the fact that the people of Quebec, on account of the lack of French employees, cannot get proper justice, .and in what I have stated I am perfectly right. I am sure, however, it is impossible for the administration to do any better so far as the operation of the road is concerned.
The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Car-veil) spoke this afternoon about sidings. I know something about the way in which sidings are obtained on the Intercolonial. The old method used to be satisfactory, but that has been changed during the last few years. Ido not object to the way in which the matter is conducted so far as the big companies are concerned. The big companies have the means to pay the expenses in connection with the building of a siding, which runs into from $500 to $1,000, but in the case of poor settlers, who very often want sidings along the Intercolonial, I think the old method should be reverted to; that is, those sidings should be built by the railway and at the expense of the railway, because a poor farmer asking for a siding is not able to pay $500 or $1,000 to a railway to build a siding. The Government would, therefore, do well to make a distinction between a siding built for a big company and one built for a private party, such as a poor settler or farmer in my province.
I would like to make a suggestion to the minister in connection with the running of the big engines that we call Santa Fe
and Mikado on that part of the line between Mont Joli and Campbellton. Those engines are too large to run over that part of the road. The men whom we engage as firemen cannot stand the work on those big engines; they have to shovel ten to twelve tons of coal every day, and that is too severe a strain for a man unless he is as strong as two ordinary men. I would prefer that smaller engines be used on that part of the road, because it is physically impossible for firemen to stand the work, the reason being that there are too many grades on that part of the road, and the grades are so heavy it takes a long time to run the 105 miles between Mont Joli and Campbellton. On other parts of the road east of Campbellton and west of Mont Joli, the runs are shorter, the road is more level, and the men. are better able to stand the strain and fulfil their duties. I have heard complaints from firemen who have been working on those engines, and they all say they cannot stand the work they have to perform on account of the size of those engines.
In reference to section 302 of Bill 13, I see in the schedule of this Bill that this section is included-
The CHAIRMAN Order. I wish to remind the hon. member that we are discussing section 4 of Bill No. 118, and the hon. gentleman's remarks must be relevant
to this section, and he is not in order in making a general speech.
I have no objection, but I will come back to it.

The question of the Intercolonial and its management is so very, very important to myself and the people I represent, I am afraid I should be regarded as indifferent to their interests if I did not say anything about the very important question now before this committee. In dealing with the Intercolonial we are dealing with a teTm of Confederation as laid down in the constitution. I wish to refer to section 145 of the British North America Act:
Inasmuch as the provinces of Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick have joined in a declaration that the construction of the Intercolonial Railway is essential to the consolidation of the Union of British North America, and to the assent thereto of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, and have consequently agreed that provision should be made for its immediate construction by the Government of Canada ; therefore in order to give effect to that agreement, it shall be the duty of the Government and Parliament of Canada to provide for the commencement within six months after

the union, of a railway connecting the River St. Lawrence with the city of Halifax in Nova Scotia, and for the construction thereof without intermission, and the completion thereof with all practicable speed.
The minister will observe that the Intercolonial is just as much a term of Confederation as the educational section in regard to the separate schools in the province of Quebec and the educational section relating to the province of Ontario. The building of it is one of the terms of Confederation.

1 thought it was the
running of it.

There is not much good in a railway, unless it is run, and the conception and the true meaning of this section is that the road shall be built, and that it shall always continue under the full and absolute control of the people as represented by the members in this House. It is not, and never was the intention of this term of Confederation that the road could be built and then passed over to some 'control over which this Parliament would have no supervision. I submit, therefore, *that if we introduce a new element into the management of this road which lessens the power of the representatives of the people over this road, we are tampering with a term of Confederation, as New Brunswick and Nova Scotia would not have come into (Confederation except for this bargain. That is laid down in the Act itself, and .so important was it that this section was put in the Act.
Mr. (COCHRANE:	Is it any different
from the terms on which British Columbia came into Confederation, when the Canadian Pacific was proposed to be buiilt?

I am sure British Columbia insisted very strenuously on the terms of Confederation being carried out, and one of the great tasks which the late Sir John (Macdonald had to perform, with great energy, and under very great difficulty, was to insist upon keeping good faith with British Columbia, and helping to build the Canadian Pacific Railway long before the people of this country were really in a financial position to do it. But that provision was in the terms of Confederation with British Columbia, and Sir John Macdonald was determined that no fault could be found with him, or his Government, that they did not keep faith with British Columbia; and the promise to British Columbia was fulfilled and absolutely and

fully carried out, and we never heard any complaint.
Were the same conditions not imposed as in the ease of the Maritime Provinces? There was nothing about the road, or rates, or anything else.

There is nothing i.n the British North America Aet about British Columbia coming in or staying out. Confederation was an actuality, a complete thing, before British Columbia came in, and Confederation would have gone on as it was whether British Columbia came in or stayed out. The terms on which British Columbia and Prince Edward Island came in, and the province of Manitoba was created, were separate and distinct contracts. Bach of those provinces came in with the body of Confederation. (But the original Confederation and the basic principles of the compact of Confederation embodied in the British North America Act are the parent of the whole business, and are, therefore, different from any branches or extensions which came afterward. I submit, the contract of Confederation and the statute upon which the whole fabric is based is different from the contract which Confederation, as represented by the King, made with another province. There is that very fundamental difference between the terms of Confederation itself and any terms Confederation may have made with British Columbia, or Prince Edward Island, or any province coming into the union. I mention this to show that it is a very serious thing to interfere in any way with the rights which the people have under the terms of the union. I submit, further, that the Intercolonial railway, with its management, is a very old institution. Confederation is 50 years old, and I do not know how long after Confederation it was before we had the Intercolonial. They certainly commenced building the Intercolonial shortly after Confederation, and it has been running ever since. Taken all in all I think it has given fair satisfaction to the people, and if the purposes of this new legislation is to impose a greater tax upon the people of the Maritime Provinces, or those who have to deal with the road, I would have to protest against it. I have not the lack of faith in the management of the Intercolonial by the department that some people might have. No institution is perfect, every institution has its faults; but I think for the last 50 years this road has been running that fair satisfaction has been given to the people. It is a sort of home institution. The people can approach

the management through their representatives, and, although ministers are sometimes a little domineering and high-and-mighty, after all they have their lucid moments, and we can approach them and put our views before them. We .are afraid of them all the time, but sometimes they are afraid of us, and we get some things done. Fortunately they have to come down to the House with their estimates, and are called upon to give us some explanations, and the people in that way have an opportunity of getting close to the management of their own road.
I am afraid that so far as concerns the part of the country I come from, if another tyrant is introduced iin the shape of this Railway Board, the people will complain that it is a new institution about which they do not know anything, and it will take them a great many years to learn how to approach it. I am sure the minister will understand that the distance between the operation of his road away down in Cape Breton and a court which sits In Ottawa, is very far, and a great drawback particularly for the people from the extreme eastern part of Nova Scotia. A man will put up with a great deal of inconvenience before he will come here to appear before the board. If it is the 'intention to raise the rates on the Intercolonial higher than they are, it will materially interfere with large industrial undertakings in our part of the country. Under war conditions, we should try to get along the best we can, and take mutual obligations and mutual burdens in order to keeps the wheels of industry going as well as possible. It is well known that we are largely dependent on the Intercolonial now to get our coal away. If the fact that we could not sell our coal was the only trouble it would not be so bad, but we have thousands of men, women and children dependent on the coal mines, and if the coal cannot be sold, the mines cannot be operated. I protest as vigorously as I can against raising the rate 31.40 a ton on coal in war times, when the King has taken our ships and put them in other places-where they .are necessary of course, but they are taken away from the purposes for which our companies had them, that of carrying away our coal. This Government makes it practically impossible for us to sell coal to any advantage when they impose 31.40 per ton extra upon the carrying of the coal to the places where we have to sell it. I appeal to the minister through you, Sir, that this matter should be considered, and that the fuel inspector
or fuel agent of the Government who is looking after it, should be consulted .by the Government and the matter taken up seriously to see if there is not some way by which we can go back to the normal rates so that our people will be able to compete. I have it on the authority of our coal managers that with this extra rate of J1.40 a ton, competing with American coals at Montreal and other places is absolutely out of the question, and means the closing down of our mines, when we have no ships; and the closing down of our mines means that our men are out of work and cannot support their families.
One of the mines in your section refused to sell us coal, because they have not any to spare.
Which mine is that?
One of the mines owned by the Nova Scotia Steel and Coal Company.
Perhaps you would not pay them enough.
That was not the reason they gave; they said they could not spare it.

I would be very glad to know they are so busy at their mines and with their sales that they cannot sell coal to the road. I am well acquainted with their shipping facilities, and they say they have no vessels. The Intercolonial is the only railroad there, and if they will not sell coal to the Intercolonial, and cannot get it to the great centres such as Montreal and Toronto, I do not know what they are doing with it. I am instructed by some of the managers that they are really up against a difficulty ydiich they do not know how to overcome. I wish to put myself on record as saying that while there have been some complaints about the management of the road, it has been doing fairly well. It is the people's railway, and it must continue as the people's railway, and must be managed by the people. The Minister of Railways, and this committee, and this Government, may as well make up their minds once for all that while any property is the property of the people, the representatives of the people must have something to say about it, and that the management whether for good or ill, must be subject to this Parliament and subject to the voice of the people. If we aTe going to run railways, or have government ownership, we may as well make up our minds that we

cannot admit any tyranny, any power about which we have nothing to say, into the ownership of our property. I think there will be less politics in the matter as we go along, but to shift it onto the shoulders of some board which we appoint ourselves and in regard to which we have nothing to say, is impossible.
Dealing with section 4, I would say as a lawyer that any talk of imposing penalties upon His Majesty is absolutely out of the question. Of course, it is His Majesty only in theory, but that theory is exceedingly important. All power, as far as our courts are concerned, is centered in the King, and it is in the name of the King that we have the courts. The humblest magistrate cannot bring a man before him under a summons or a warrant except in the name of the King. The King is the central power, and it is altogether out of the question that he will summon himself into his own court. The Parliament is a King's court, and as far as Canada is concerned, the King's highest court. We are sitting here by authority of the King. It is entirely out of the question that we shall constitute a court under this Act by which the King will be subject to penalty. Whatever other way it may be done, we must keep the source of power around which the. whole machinery of justice Tevolves absolutely free from any entanglement of that kind, and if there is any punishment to ;be imposed under the operation of this Act it must be something separate, apart and distinct from the name of the King, so that any proceedings instituted can be instituted in the name of the King.

Will the minister not take into consideration the points brought forward by my hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvell) and myself on this section?
Mr. M1IDDLEBRO:	I had intended to
move an amendment to section 4. Perhaps I might do i-t now. There is a good deal in the point raised by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) and others, that there appears to be no penalty or no sanction for not doing what the board orders. I think perhaps if there were some sanction or penalty on the minister for not carrying out the orders of the board, he would be put more in the nature of a private corporation, and I think the officials of the company would be more likely to carry out the directions of the board. I think they should be subject to such penalty as the board may see fit to impose upon them in case they do not carry out its
[Mr. McKenzie.J
orders. For instance, section 34, subsection 3, the general Railway Act, says:
The Board may by regulation or order provide penalties, when not already provided in this Act, to which every company or person who offends against any regulation or order made by the Board shall be liable.
Subsection 4 says:
The imposition of any such penalty shall not lessen or affect any other liability which any company or person may have incurred.
That imposes on the minister the duty of carrying out the order which the board makes and in addition to that I think there should be some penalty ffir not doing so. I would therefore, with the consent of the minister, move:
That clause 4 be struck out and that the following be substituted therefor:
"Notwithstanding anything contained herein, or , in the Railway Act, His Majesty shall not, nor shall the Minister of Railways and Canals, be liable to any fine or penalty except such as may be imposed by the Board, and no orcert or judgment of the Board under or in consequence of which His Majesty would have to pay or expend any money shall have any force or effect until it has been approved by the Governor in Council.
The effect of that would be that if the board made an order against the Minister of Railways and Canals under this Act he would have to comply with that order and pay such fine as the board imposed.

The amendment suggested by the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Middlebro) may be all right but he has not touched the real gravamen of the latter part of the clause. The latter part of the clause does not provide for fines but it provides for carrying out the order of the board regarding the expenditure of money. The board may order that the Intercolonial shall construct a siding, perhaps costing $100, $200; we feel that there should be some power to compel the Intercolonial to carry out the instructions of the board. As the clause is drafted the minister is not compelled to carry out the instructions of the board, and I do not think the amendment proposed by my hon. friend meets that.

The Government is in a different position from an individual. We have to have money voted by Parliament or go to the Governor in Council to get permission. A minister cannot spend money if it is not voted.
You have large sums of money voted for general purposes with regard to which you could exercise some discretion.
Very little. The hon. gentleman knows that in passing the railway estimates- we have to say what everything is for. We do not get a blanket vote.

My hon. friend takes a large vote which is nothing more than a cross entry. He receives $15,000,000 from the railway in the year and when he comes to Parliament he takes a vote of practically what he anticipates will be the income of the railway for the year.
No, we take a lump sum for operation. It is not at all available for improvements.
My hon. friend makes a distinction between what he takes for capital and what he takes for operation.
At page 52 of the estimates my hon. friend takes $6,875,000 for Canadian Government railways chargeable to capital.
He takes more than that.

Then, at page 54 he
takes $23,000,000.
That is for operation.
My hon. friend has taken a vote of $23,000,000 this year.
That is for operation, not construction.
He takes a special vote on capital account.

On page 52 there is for:
Construction and betterments, $6,500,000.
That is for capital expenditure? '
Yes.

My hon. friend takes that capital vote and he takes the ordinary vote which is nothing more than a cross entry. The board, save in most exceptional cases, would only require the fulfilment of an -order dependent on the money being voted by Parliament. Therefore, that difficulty does not arise. The amendment of my hon. friend from North Grey (Mr. Mid-dlebro) does not offer any solution. If the Act is to be workable the party upon whom the onus must be thrown for carrying out the orders of the board is the general manager of the government railways.
He is not allowed to spend money without orders.
If the orders of the board are to -be fulfilled he is the man who actually spends the money. My hon. friend does not thin-k that he is the general manager?
I authorize it.

The hon. gentleman authorizes it. But, we are arguing in a circle and we get back to this, that you are going to have the board make orders and you are going to put parties to the expense of going before the board to get an order, when the whole thing will be nugatory. Why do you not put the onus on the general manager of carrying the order of the board into effect? Why should not the people who are operating the Intercolonial be in the same position as the people who are operating the Canadian Pacific, Grand Trunk or Canadian Northern? The amendment proposed by the hon. member for North Grey does not reach the situation at all.
It certainly is admitting penalties.
It is admitting penalties, but I doubt whether the language is sufficiently apt to expressly override the common law rule that there is no penalty. But it may be so.
It takes out clause 4 and admits a penalty.
What is the objection to putting the onus on the general manager?

Because he is not allowed to spend money without permission, nor is the minister. The minister may get an Order in Council passed, but if he does not do so the Auditor General will not permit the bills to be paid.
The Auditor General would have sufficient authority under -an order of the board?
I do not know whether he would or not.

I must protest against the amendment proposed to section 4, absolutely. The section was bad enough before. It suggested that a penalty might be imposed upon the King. But here we have -a court created by the King, deriving its authority from the King, and -it is authorized to impose a penalty upon the King. It is absolutely absurd, and I appeal to you and the committee that at least it should

not be adopted until we have the opinion of the Justice Department about it. There is no such law anywhere in the Empire, nor has it ever been attempted to pass such a law. It is a glaring absurdity, and I would be ashamed to be a member of a legislature that would pass such an enactment in the twentieth century.

I understand the position taken by the hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie), and I think it is right. It is absolutely illogical that you should start proceedings against the King, at the instigation of the King, in an ordinary court. The hon. member for Pic-tou (Mr. Macdonald) has given us a solution. We have been labouring under a great misapprehension about the uselessness and nonsense of taking money out of the treasury and putting it back into the other pocket. But that is not the case under the provisions of the Railway Act, because if a penalty is imposed upon a railway company it is treated as is any other fine. The 'Summary Convictions Act and the General Criminal Code provide for the disposition of the penalty. It does not go to the Dominion, but partly to the municipalities. Therefore there is no reason why the Intercolonial should not be fined.
A fine imposed by the Railway Board does snot go to the municipalities.

I am not speaking of
such a fine as that but of the fine imposed -upon a person who, for breach of an order of the board, comes under the general law of the land. While it is inconsistent to lay an information in the name of the King against the King, there will he no difficulty in laying information in the name of the King against the manager of the Canadian Government railways. If the manager is fined he pays the fine out of moneys in his hands belonging to the Government, and in that way justice is satisfied and it is hoped there will not be a repetition of the events. I quite agree with the hon. member fox North Cape Breton, that the present situation would be absolutely illogical if you attempt to fine the King, but you could fine the railway company in the name of the general manager.
'Mr. COCHRANE: Suppose we allow the clause to stand to-night.
Section stands.
On section 5-Rules for practice and procedure :

iMr. MACDONALD:	il move to amend
this section by adding at the end thereof the words " not inconsistent with the terms of the Railway Act ".
Amendment agreed to and section as amended agreed to.
On section 6-Sections of the Government Railways Act repealed:

I beg leave to move:
That clause 6 of the Bill he struck out and the following clause be substiuted in lieu thereof:
"6. (1) The following sections of the Government Railways Act, Revised Statutes of Canada, 1906, Chapter thirty-six, are hereby repealed:
"Sections 7 to 9 both inclusive, 15 to 45 both inclusive, 58, 61 and 64 to 79 both inclusive.
"(2) In case of any inconsistency between the provisions of the Government Railways Act and the sections of the Railway Act, as set out in the schedule to this Act, the provisions of the said sections shall prevail."

I do not think the minister should ask us to adopt that amendment without our first having an opportunity of considering it. I imagine the minister will also make some changes in the -schedule, and I would suggest that he give notice tonight of what changes he purposes to make. I have no doubt that they will be accepted, but we should have opportunity of examining them.

The proposed new
clause is considered to be in better legal form. Sections 7 to 9 of the' Government Railways Act are repealed and are replaced by sections 245, 246 and 247 of the Railways Act, which appear in the schedule. They relate to bridges. Sections 46 to 49 are restored, as they constitute the authority of the Governor in Council to impose tolls. These will be subject to the approval of the board.
That is a rather large order for one to carry in one's head. I would suggest that the minister give notice of all the changes and then we shall have an opportunity of examining them.
I understand that that amendment covers practically all the objections which the hon. member for Carleton made this aftempon.
I must have referred to twenty or thirty clauses; this refers to only three or four.
I have ,a list of the clauses that my hon. friend referred to.
I do not want to be unfair, but I really wish to make the Act as workable as possible-

I will give notice of

I will now make a remark that I was going to make a few minutes ago. I see that this Bill is going to be in line with Bill No. 13, that is, that certain sections in Bill 13 are to be included in this Bill. Among them is section 302. The Minister of Railways is reported in Hansard of the 23rd of July last as having made these remarks:
Mr. Cochrane:	On the 18th July I accepted
an amendment prepared by my hon. friend from Rouville and proposed by the hon. gentleman from Rimouski, which read as follows:
"All railway employees on local passenger trains running in the province of Quebec, having to deal with the travelling public, shall be conversant with the English and French languages from and after January 1, 1919."
There has been strong objection to this amendment on the ground that it would cut men out of their seniority. For Instance, a man running on a freight train to Prescott or Brockville would be prevented from being promoted, say, to a passenger train running to

Montreal, because he was not able to speak French. I feel that the amendment suggested by the member for Muskoka (Mr. Wright) will meet the situation far better. I move that section 302 be amended by adding thereto the following as subsection 3 :
"After the 1st day of January, 1919, the Board may from time to time make such or-* ders and regulations as it may deem advisable to provide that all or any railway employee on local passenger trains running in the province of Quebec shall be conversant with the English and French languages."
I am sorry that the amendment thus moved has been changed. I see that I am the only member from Quebec now present. I wish we were all here, because I I know all the other hon. members from Quebec would approve what I am going to say on this subject, and of the amendment I am going to suggest to section 302 of Bill No. 118.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must remind the hon. member that we are not considering Bill No. 13; we are considering Bill No. 118.

1 wish to move an amendment to the schedule of Bill 118 as regards section 302 of the Railway Act concerning the Government railways. I wish to add to section 302 practically the same words that I proposed on the 18th of July, as follows:
All employees of government railways in the province of Quebec that have to deal with the travelling public shall be conversant with the English and French languages, and this provision to be in force from the first of January, 1919.
As this affects only the Government railway employees, there should not be any such objection as that referred to by the Minister of Railways on the 23rd of July as regards other railroads. This- would meet the approval of all the employees of the Government railways in Quebec, because I [DOT]have here a statement signed by four of the presidents of their societies from Montreal to Campbellton. They all approve this amendment saying that it would be largely in the interest of the travelling public. The statement is dated 28th July, 1917, and reads:
The hon. member for Rimouski has caused to be inserted in the Bill No. 13' entitled: An Act for the consolidation of the railway laws of Canada, on the 18 th instant, an amendment which reads as follows:
" All railway employees on local passenger trains running in the province of Quebec, having to deal with the travelling public, shall be conversant with the English and French languages from and after January 1, 1919."
Now, on Juy 23rd instant, this amendment, although it had been adopted by the House, was dropped and another one has been substituted to it which does not give any satisfaction. The

speechtext:
The amendment moved by the hon. gentleman from Rimouski is not relevant. I find the following in Bourinot:
Amendments to Bills must strictly relate to the Bill which the House has by its order resolved upon considering.
So that I must rule that this amendment is not in order.
I assume that section 7 stands as it is.
